newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Bunds seen climbing after battering T-notes.
newsitem.headline: German Bunds seen climbing after battering T-notes.

text.p: German Bunds shot forward against their American counterparts after non-farm payrolls rose by 250,000 in August, pushing the yield spread between the two to its widest point in well over two years.

The spread between Bunds and T-notes stood at minus 79 basis points shortly after the data, the widest spread since since May 11, 1994 when it stood at minus 82 basis points. The spread narrowed to minus 74 points late in the day.
Analysts said that spread could widen even further amid signs of higher U.S. interest rates at the same time that some think that German interest rates may still fall.
"People seem to love their Bunds," said Hans Nordstrom, trader at BMP Wertpapiere und Optionen GmbH. "Bunds should climb still higher."
Indeed, traders said the December Bund DTB contract could climb to 97.00 next week, although it faces resistance at 96.75. In late trade, the contract was up four basis points at 96.59.

Nordstrom and others said that although the Bundesbank cut the repo rate by a surprisingly large 30 basis points to 3.0 percent in late August, there was still speculation of yet further rate cuts, supporting Bunds.
"The major risk on Bunds is if the market takes the view that no more rate cuts are coming," said Claudio Demolli, analyst at Stone & McCarthy in London. "I do not see that happening any time soon."
Now that U.S. jobs data are out of the way, traders said the focus will turn to German consumer price figures which are due next week and U.S. producer price data which are due next Thursday.
Even if the figures point to faster economic growth, some expect the current bullish sentiment to lead traders to jump on any dip in prices.

Traders said the Bund future contract looks good from a technical view point. The September contract had corrected a full point from a high near 98.30 in mid-August, erasing any worries about what had been a quick rally in the market.

The December contract, which is trading almost exactly 100 points below the September contract, meanwhile climbed easily through 96.50 and looks to have little trouble breaking through weak resistance at 96.65.
One trader said the Bundesbank will continue to talk up the chances of lower rates so as to help the long-end of the yield curve and lower the cost of investing.
